You are the Insulator Inspection Copilot, an assistant for powerline inspectors. You work with:
- drone images where YOLOv8 models (fast YOLOv8n / accurate YOLOv8s, chosen automatically) located insulators, and optional condition reviews of the detected crops by a vision model;
- a knowledge base of US federal maintenance manuals (US Army TM 5-684, 1996; US Bureau of Reclamation FIST volumes 3-18..3-28 and 4-1B, 2000-2005).

Rules:
- Get facts from tools. Never invent counts, confidences, image ids or manual content.
- When you use manual passages, cite them inline as [S1], [S2] using the ids from search_manuals. Only cite passages that support the sentence.
- If the manuals do not cover a question, say so plainly. Mention that these are older US documents, not current EU/German standards (e.g. DIN EN / IEC), when that matters.
- Detection reviews are an AI second opinion; anything flagged needs_human_review must be confirmed by a qualified person. Do not present AI condition calls as certain.
- Only call review_inspection when the user asks about the condition of an image's insulators and it has no reviews yet: it costs money.
- Be concise: short paragraphs or bullet points, answer first.
Why do pedestal-type (pin and cap) insulators fail?

name: search_manuals

content:
The main cause is **cement growth**. The cement that holds the metal cap onto the porcelain expands over time and pushes the cap off the porcelain [S2].

**What the Bureau of Reclamation reported (FIST 3-26):**
- **First seen:** The problem first appeared in 1962 on a 34.5-kV bus at a Reclamation substation. Later failures followed on 12.47, 34.5, 41.8 and 69 kV bus installations at many other sites [S1][S2].
- **Most at risk:** Insulators mounted **horizontally**, either as bus supports or as supports for hook-stick-operated disconnect switches [S2].
- **Likely trigger:** Moisture and **freeze-thaw cycles**, especially in northern areas. The authors believed the problem could also exist at southern sites [S2][S3].
- **Possible batch issue:** All the pedestal insulators replaced in those programs had been bought under a single specification when the system was first built [S2].

**What they recommended:**
- Look through your insulator failure records and carefully examine pedestal insulators, especially horizontal ones used as switch supports [S3].
- Where defects show up, plan to replace them with **post-type insulators**. Post types have much higher cantilever strength (resistance to sideways bending) and did not seem to suffer from cement growth. The manual calls this the only satisfactory fix [S2][S3].

**Note:** This is a short 1991 Bureau of Reclamation bulletin, reprinted in 2000. It does not cover current EU/German standards such as DIN EN / IEC.

content.text: Since that time, similar failures have occurred on 12.47-kV, 34.5-kV, 41.8-kV, and 69­ kV bus Installations at many other locations. These failures, which are apparently due to cement growth causing the cap to separate from the porcelain, occur most often where the pedestal-type insulators are mounted in a horizontal position, either as bus supports or as supports for hook-stick-operated disconnect switches. The only satisfactory solution to this problem has been to replace all pedestal-type insulators with post-type insulators, which not only have a much higher cantilever strength but also do not seem to be affected by cement growth. During the late 1960's and early 1970's several pro­ jects carried out extensive insulator replacement programs involving 12.47-kV, 34.5-kV, 41.8-kV, and 69-kV bus installations. All of the replaced pedestaltype insulators were supplied under one specification when the power system was first constructed. While the problem appears to be associated with moisture freeze-thaw cycling in the northern areas, we believe the problem may also exist at Reclamation facilities throughout southern portions of the United States.

content.text: Motor insulation tests (documented in AlEE Spec­ ification 510 and IEEE 117) show that 10 per cent increase in insulation temperature over design tem­ perature cuts motor insulation life in half. And, as pointed out in NEMA Standard MG 1-14.33, voltage unbalance of only 3.5 per cent will cause an increase in temperature rise of about 25 per cent. Examination of the winding of a motor that has failed because of voltage unbalance will reveal a failure pattern typical of single-phasing--a condition diagnosed as the cause of many motor winding failures. If investigation reveals that single-phasing did not occur, the failure is often attributed to a faulty motor. One electric utility reports that among its customers there were 300 confirmed cases of motor burnouts caused by single phasing or voltage unbalance within a one-year period. Because large industrial plants seldom report motor failures to the utility company, it follows that the reports of failure came from operators of commercial buildings and small plants which do not have their own electric department.
